blocks.text: Results: Socioeconomic Ranks of Nobel Laureate Childhoods, 1901–2023

nodes.text: The analysis dataset consists of 714 winners from 44 countries over a period of 123 years. About 4% of winners are women, 35% grew up in the U.S., and an additional 12% in the United Kingdom.
Figure

nodes.label: fig:rank_histograms
nodes.text: Figure 1

plots the distribution of the father ranks of the laureates. 68% of winners have fathers above the 90ᵗʰ income percentile in their birth country, 71% have fathers above the 90ᵗʰ education percentile, and 84% above the 90ᵗʰ global income percentile. In all three cases, more than half of winners are from the top 5%. The mean laureate has a father at the 87th income percentile, the 89th education percentile, and the 94th global income percentile.

blocks.label: fig:rank_histograms
blocks.caption: Distribution of Socioeconomic Ranks of Fathers of Nobel Laureates

nodes.text: Panel A of Appendix Figure

shows the ten most common occupations held by the fathers of laureates, along with the occupation's census population share. Business owners, professors, physicians, and scientists feature most prominently. Relative to their occupational shares, professors are overrepresented by a factor of 82.4, physicians and engineers by 12.1 each, and business owners by a factor of 2.8.

blocks.text: Results: Heterogeneity by Gender, Field and Region

nodes.text: Female laureates came from more educated families than male laureates, but the difference estimates are imprecise, given there have been only 28 female winners in the sciences in the 123 years of the Nobel Prize's history (Table

nodes.label: tab:heterogeneity
nodes.text: Table 2

, Panel A). The average female laureate has a national education rank that is 4.6 rank points higher than the average male laureate (p=0.05), and is more likely to be from a top-10% or top-20% education family (p=0.13 and p=0.06 respectively). The national income estimates point in the same direction but are not statistically significant.
On the global income rank measures, women's ranks are very similar to men's.
There are no statistically significant gender differences in the long-run rank trend, but the estimate is imprecise because there are so few female laureates (Appendix Table

blocks.label: tab:heterogeneity
blocks.caption: Heterogeneity in Socioeconomic Rank of Fathers of Nobel Laureates

nodes.text: Table

nodes.label: tab:heterogeneity
nodes.text: Table 2

C shows the regional pattern of winners' ranks. Laureates from the U.S. tend to come from less elite backgrounds than winners from Europe and the rest of the world, suggesting more equal access to opportunity in the sciences in the United States. 39% of U.S. laureates come from the bottom 90% of their national income distributions, compared with 27% in the rest of the world, with similar differences for other measures. The regional differences are highly statistically significant. Appendix Table
shows regression estimates from just the United States against the rest of the world.
In Appendix Table

, we examine whether the time trends vary by the subgroups examined here. The point estimates suggest some heterogeneity: access to scientific opportunity is rising the most for women; in chemistry and physiology; and in Western Europe. But these differences are imprecise and joint tests of equal trends across subgroups are for the most part not statistically significant.

There are six laureates whose fathers were also Nobel laureates — one of whom (William Lawrence Bragg) shared the prize with his father (William Henry Bragg) — and one winner (Irène Joliot-Curie), whose parents were both laureates.
The frequency distribution of father occupations is largely similar across the different prize categories. Appendix Tables
and
show prize and census share statistics for additional occupation groups. These are broken down by Nobel field in Appendix Table
. Notably, there are no high education groups with substantial underrepresentation among the laureates, nor high income groups with substantial overrepresentation.
Appendix Table
shows that these estimates are robust to alternate father coding choices as above. Panel B of Appendix Figure
shows the most common father occupations among the set of female laureates.
Appendix Table
shows the list of countries by classification region.

references.text: Bell, A., Chetty, R., Jaravel, X., Petkova, N., Van Reenen, J. (2019). Who Becomes an Inventor in America? The Importance of Exposure to Innovation. The Quarterly Journal of Economics.

body.text: These are the occupations that show up most often among the fathers of Nobel laureates. The blue bar is the laureates' share; the grey bar is how common the same occupation is in the general working population. The gap between them — shown as a multiplier — is how over-represented that background is.

body.text: This graph compares the laureate share with a given father occupation to the raw population share with that occupation.

This is the appendix version of the main trend figure, with the horizontal axis showing the father's birth cohort rather than the year the prize was awarded. We prefer prize year for the primary analysis because, for the most recent birth cohorts, we do not yet observe everyone who may go on to win a Nobel Prize.

Rather than average rank, this graph shows the share of laureates whose fathers ranked below the 80th and below the 90th percentiles. A rising line means laureates are increasingly drawn from outside the top of the distribution.

This table tests robustness to alternative ways of coding some laureate ranks. For business owners, we adjust ranks based on whether the reported business was small or large. For education, we replace the occupational rank with the direct information reported by the laureate. We prefer the occupational education in the main analysis, because laureates may selectively report their parents' education in their biographies.

annotations.title: Global rank estimates: robustness to national occupation distribution adjustment

body.text: This table shows that calculating global ranks in a slightly different manner — using the 1950 U.S. occupation distribution for all years — does not materially affect the findings on the trend in laureate global SES ranks.
This table shows the assignments made between occupations and scientific disciplines.

These figures show how the parent-child field match changes under stricter and looser definitions of the field match: for professors only, for non-professors, and for father occupations with weaker topical links.

props.note: Grey bars: simulated distribution of parent-child field match shares across 10,000 random reassignments. This shows the expected distribution if laureates are randomly assigned to fields. Dashed line: simulation mean (expected under null). Red line: empirically observed match share. p-value = fraction of simulations ≥ observed.
